topic.angle: A random number nudges your estimate

card.title: A random number can steer your guess

body.claim: In a classic experiment, people who saw a high random number guessed higher than people who saw a low one.
body.why: People watched a wheel rigged to land on 10 or 65, then estimated the percentage of African countries in the United Nations. Those who saw 10 guessed about 25% on average, and those who saw 65 guessed about 45%. Our estimates drift toward whatever number we saw first. This is called anchoring.

probes.question: True or false: an obviously random number can still shift people's estimates.
The pull of a first number on later estimates is called ____.

image_brief.show: A ship anchor, or a roulette-style wheel (illustration is fine)

claims.claim: In a classic experiment, people who saw a high random number guessed higher than people who saw a low one.
claims.quote: Participants whose wheel stopped on 10 guessed lower values (25% on average) than participants whose wheel stopped at 65 (45% on average)

claims.claim: People watched a wheel rigged to land on 10 or 65.
claims.quote: observed a roulette wheel that was predetermined to stop on either 10 or 65

claims.claim: Participants estimated the percentage of African countries in the United Nations.
claims.quote: participants were asked to estimate the percentage of African countries in the United Nations

claims.claim: Those who saw 10 guessed about 25% on average, those who saw 65 about 45%.
claims.quote: guessed lower values (25% on average) than participants whose wheel stopped at 65 (45% on average)

claims.claim: Estimates drift toward a first number seen; this is called anchoring.
claims.quote: judgments or decisions are influenced by a reference point or "anchor"

claims.claim: Probe: an obviously random number can still shift estimates (true).
claims.quote: Anchoring persists even when the anchor is implausible or clearly irrelevant (e.g., spinning a random wheel)

claims.claim: Probe: the pull of a first number on later estimates is called anchoring.
claims.quote: The anchoring effect is a psychological phenomenon in which an individual's judgments or decisions are influenced by a reference point
